data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories inevitably smuggles in induction; Popper's attempt to separate 'corroboration' from 'probability' is semantically unstable when applied to action.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one can demonstrate a form of action that does not rely on expectations of future regularity, this claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' can be shown to mean something other than 'expectation of utility,' the inductive charge is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"To prefer Theory A over Theory B for action is to assert that A is more likely to yield successful outcomes than B.
